summary: Barr Yaron, partner at Amplify, presents findings from the 2026 State of AI Engineering survey, conducted in partnership with Notion and Vercel with 1,048 respondents. She notes the field changes so rapidly that major announcements occur even during the presentation, making the annual survey a tool to cut through noise and understand what practitioners actually do. On workforce, AI engineering is described as a discipline rather than a job title, touching founders, CTOs, engineers, and product people. For the third year, respondents skew toward senior software engineers who are newer to AI—over half of those with 10+ years of software experience have three years or less of AI experience, and the median new engineer has nearly as much AI experience as the median 10-year veteran. On modalities, text dominates. Audio has the highest intent-to-adopt ratio at 56% (up from 37% last year). Image generation usage doubled from 18% to 36%, illustrating what happens when a modality crosses a quality threshold. On model strategy, 94% use closed models, 45% use open-weight, and over 90% of open-weight users also use closed models—augmentation, not replacement. Quality dominates model choice; the open vs. closed debate was a top-three consideration for only 5%. Reliability has become a threshold requirement rather than a differentiator. 87% of teams use multiple models, routing by task type, comparing outputs, or routing by cost, and over half are starting to standardize on fewer AI tools—not models, but platform layers. On cost, it is a first-class engineering constraint: 40% say it regularly shapes how ambitiously they use AI, and 36% say it sometimes does. Cost and token usage are the number-two monitored production metric, treated like an SLA beneath quality. On agents, 95% of respondents use agents (roughly double last year), and 89% of those agents have write access (up from 52%), shifting from reading and summarizing to taking actions inside systems. Control mechanisms remain blunt—human-in-the-loop approvals and gated permissions lead, with task decomposition, retrieval, memory, and sandboxing scattered below. Two-thirds say hallucination or losing context mid-task is the primary agent frustration. On infrastructure, evals remain the number-one stack challenge by a thin and shrinking margin, with 96% reporting stack problems but disagreeing on which one. The vibe review is still the top evaluation method. Build vs. buy varies by layer: inference and model serving is the most bought layer, prompt management is mostly built in-house (61%), and fine-tuning remains largely unadopted. Those who bought aren't looking to build and vice versa. On team impact, 97% report a net positive effect on their organization—driven not just by speed but by cheaper failure, more experimentation, more prototypes, more bets. However, over nine in ten report negative downstream effects, most commonly erosion of deep technical skills and codebase understanding. 81% say AI is blurring the line between engineering and product/design/marketing roles. Over a third of teams have non-developers shipping features (mostly smaller, mostly internal), with 17% saying non-developers regularly ship customer-facing features. 76% say AI boosted their job satisfaction, but 59% fear today's AI code creates long-term liabilities, and only a third call software engineering a solved problem. On five-year bets, 67% expect a leading lab will declare AGI (press release, not achievement), only 9% bet on Transformers remaining state-of-the-art, and the most divisive question was AI compute in space (36% yes, 38% no).
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Survey Context
sections.summary: Barr Yaron introduces the 2026 State of AI Engineering survey, conducted in partnership with Notion and Vercel. She notes the field changes so fast that announcements happen mid-presentation, which is exactly why the annual survey exists—to cut through noise and understand what practitioners actually do. 1,048 respondents participated.

sections.title: The AI Engineering Workforce
sections.summary: AI engineering is a discipline rather than a job title, spanning founders, CTOs, engineers, and product people. For the third year, respondents skew toward senior engineers newer to AI: over half of those with 10+ years of software experience have three years or less of AI experience. The median new engineer has nearly as much AI experience as the median 10-year veteran.

sections.title: Current Modalities and Adoption
sections.summary: Text dominates as a modality. Audio has the highest intent-to-adopt ratio at 56% (up from 37% last year), indicating accelerating interest. Image generation usage doubled from 18% to 36%, demonstrating what happens when a modality crosses a quality threshold thanks to improved models.

sections.title: Model Strategy: Closed vs. Open-Weight
sections.summary: 94% use closed models, 45% use open-weight models, with over 90% of open-weight users also using closed models—augmentation, not replacement. Quality dominates model choice; the open vs. closed debate was a top-3 consideration for only 5%. Reliability has become a threshold requirement. 87% use multiple models, routing by task type, comparing outputs, or routing by cost. Over half are standardizing on fewer AI tools (platform, not model standardization).

sections.title: Cost as an Engineering Constraint
sections.summary: Cost is now a first-class engineering constraint. 40% say it regularly shapes how ambitiously they use AI, and 36% say it sometimes does—roughly three out of four respondents. Cost and token usage is the number-two monitored production metric, treated like an SLA right beneath quality.

sections.title: The Rise of Agentic Workflows
sections.summary: 95% of respondents use agents (roughly double last year), and 89% of those agents have write access (up from 52%). Agents are no longer reading and summarizing—they are taking actions inside systems. Control mechanisms remain blunt: human-in-the-loop approvals and gated permissions lead, with task decomposition, retrieval, memory, and sandboxing scattered below. Two-thirds say hallucination or losing context mid-task is the primary frustration.

sections.title: Infrastructure Challenges and Evals
sections.summary: Evals remain the number-one stack challenge by a thin and shrinking margin. 96% of respondents report stack problems but disagree on which one—creating an opportunity map for infrastructure builders. The vibe review is still the top evaluation method, unchanged from prior years.

sections.title: The Build vs. Buy Trade-off
sections.summary: Build vs. buy varies sharply by stack layer. Inference and model serving is the most bought layer. Prompt management is mostly built in-house (61%), along with product logic, RAG, and evals. Fine-tuning is the clearest 'not yet.' Those who bought aren't looking to build and vice versa.

sections.title: Impact on Engineering Culture and Teams
sections.summary: 97% report a net positive organizational effect—not just speed but cheaper failure, more experimentation, more prototypes, more bets. But over 9 in 10 report negative downstream effects, most commonly erosion of deep technical skills and codebase understanding. 81% say AI blurs the line between engineering and product/design/marketing. Over a third of teams have non-developers shipping features (mostly smaller, mostly internal), with 17% regularly shipping customer-facing features. Shipping software is no longer gated on being an engineer.

sections.title: Future Bets and Predictions
sections.summary: 76% say AI boosted job satisfaction, but 59% fear today's AI code creates long-term liabilities, and only a third call software engineering a solved problem. On five-year bets: 67% expect a leading lab will declare AGI (press release, not achievement), only 9% bet on Transformers remaining state-of-the-art, and the most divisive question was AI compute in space (36% yes, 38% no). Barr wraps up with a review of key findings: image gen doubled, audio has highest adoption intent, cost became first-class, open weights augment not replace, agents got write access with primitive guardrails, and inference is the buy market while product logic stays in-house.

limitations: Survey is a snapshot in a rapidly changing field; major announcements can occur during the presentation itself
Reliability data interpretation is ambiguous—likely a threshold requirement rather than truly unimportant, but not conclusively determined from the survey alone
Builder-heavy sample may overrepresent positive sentiment compared to broader engineering population
AGI question asks about press release declaration, not actual achievement—meaning of declaration is unclear

evidence.excerpt: the median new engineer has nearly as much AI experience as the median 10-year software veteran
evidence.supports: New engineers entering the field have AI experience comparable to veteran software engineers, because they have never known software without AI.

evidence.excerpt: 94% use closed models. 45% are using openweight models
evidence.supports: Closed model usage far exceeds open-weight usage, and open-weight models augment rather than replace closed models.

evidence.excerpt: Cost is now a first class engineering constraint
evidence.supports: Cost has become a primary factor in AI engineering decisions, not just an afterthought.

evidence.excerpt: Agents are no longer reading, summarizing, drafting. They're taking actions inside of systems.
evidence.supports: Agents have shifted from passive tasks to active system manipulation, enabled by increased write access.

evidence.excerpt: Every single year that I ask this, the answer, the number one answer is eval
evidence.supports: Evals have consistently been the top infrastructure challenge in AI engineering stacks across multiple survey years.

evidence.excerpt: 61% build it themselves. Um apparently everyone's prompts are special
evidence.supports: Prompt management is predominantly built in-house rather than bought, unlike inference infrastructure which is mostly purchased.

evidence.excerpt: 97% report a net positive effect on their organization
evidence.supports: AI has had a broadly positive impact on engineering organizations, though this coexists with negative downstream effects.

evidence.excerpt: erosion of deep technical skills and understanding of the codebase
evidence.supports: Cheap code generation has negative consequences including skill erosion and reduced codebase understanding, reported by over 90% of respondents.

evidence.excerpt: Shipping software is not gated on being an engineer anymore
evidence.supports: AI tools have democratized software creation beyond the engineering role, enabling non-developers to ship features.

evidence.excerpt: 67% expect a leading lab will declare AGI in the next five years
evidence.supports: A strong majority of practitioners believe a lab will publicly claim AGI within five years, though the meaning of such a declaration remains uncertain.
